column4: The morning that “breathes” (تَنَفَّسَ) directly joins the section’s opening dawn to its closing address to the نَفْس: the rent in darkness is figured as breath.
فَالِقُ ٱلْإِصْبَاحِ names God as the splitter of daybreak; it gives an agent to the section’s image of darkness cracking open at dawn.
The white thread becoming distinct from the black thread مِنَ ٱلْفَجْرِ makes dawn the fine separating line described in the section, not a fully lit expanse.
The oath by the night as it عسعس presents night in transition; beside 81:18 it is the same moving cover and opening morning staged in 89:4 and 89:1.
The night “when it turns its back” gives the section’s travelling night a visible departure immediately before the whitening morning of 74:34.
The morning “when it brightens” supplies the revealed side of the section’s two-part motion: night withdraws and what lay beneath becomes visible.
وَٱلَّيْلِ إِذَا يَغْشَىٰ is the section’s night-cover in its fullest action, before any rent or withdrawal has opened it.
The day “when it unveils itself” (تَجَلَّىٰ) is the answering motion to 92:1’s covering night and closely matches the section’s uncovering as night goes.
جَنَّ عَلَيْهِ ٱلَّيْلُ uses the section’s own covering root: night covers Abraham yet lets the star appear, making darkness a setting for discerning what sets from what does not.
The Night of Decree remains peace حَتَّىٰ مَطْلَعِ ٱلْفَجْرِ, so dawn is the exact boundary at which a whole night-state ends.
Seeking refuge in رَبِّ ٱلْفَلَقِ invokes the same opening by splitting that the section hears in God’s cleaving of morning, while keeping فلق distinct from فجر.
يُغْشِى ٱلَّيْلَ ٱلنَّهَارَ describes night as a cover laid over day, while يَطْلُبُهُ حَثِيثًا makes that cover move rather than remain fixed.
God “wraps” night over day and day over night; the reciprocal wrapping supplies the section’s sliding-cover mechanism in both directions.
The oath by day when it displays the sun contributes the disclosure that answers the covering action of the next ayah.
The oath by night when it covers the sun (يَغْشَىٰهَا) turns night into precisely the spread covering from which the section’s dawn must emerge.
The bright forenoon supplies the opened, illuminated pole of an oath-pair whose other pole is the still night in 93:2.
The night “when it grows still” is a specific counter-image to 89:4’s night in motion; the same night can be perceived as settled cover or departing traveller.
God makes night a garment, sleep a repose, and day a rising; this one sequence joins cover, death-like concealment, and renewed emergence.
“We made the night a garment” gives literal Qur’anic form to the section’s night spread over things as a covering.
The erased sign of night and the sight-giving sign of day connect darkness and visibility, while the reckoning of years links the succession of nights to counted time.
Moses’ appointment is thirty nights completed by ten; the explicit addition of عَشْر makes this the clearest external counterpart to the section’s counted ten nights.
The command to travel by a portion of the night uses the same س ر ي sense as 89:4, and “their appointment is the morning” makes dawn the journey’s decisive limit.
أَسْرَىٰ بِعَبْدِهِۦ لَيْلًا states the section’s dictionary sense of surā exactly: a divinely conducted journey during the night.
Travel with the family during a portion of night repeats the same س ر ي night-journey and makes movement through darkness the means of escape.
The command to take the servants by night uses the section’s س ر ي sense and leads directly to a dry path opened through the sea, joining night travel to an opening.
“Travel by night with My servants” repeats the same root and speaker-pattern as the section’s moving night, here as a saving departure before morning pursuit.
The command to journey by night with God’s servants gives the same س ر ي action and makes the darkness a passage toward deliverance.
Leaving the sea رهوا after the night journey supplies an opened passage that remains behind once the travellers have gone through, completing 44:23’s scene.
God splits the grain and date-stone before 6:96 calls Him the splitter of daybreak; hidden life and hidden morning emerge by the same فلق action.
“We removed from you your covering” (فَكَشَفْنَا عَنكَ غِطَآءَكَ) makes sight sharp on the Last Day, extending the section’s removal of a cover from physical dawn to final perception.
حِجْرًا مَّحْجُورًا is the section’s own outward, eschatological form of حِجْر: a boundary declared when the angels become visible and good news is barred from the guilty.
حِجْرًا مَّحْجُورًا names the restraining boundary between two meeting bodies of water, giving the section’s inner wall a concrete cosmic analogue.
The wall with a gate has mercy inside and punishment outside; it makes an eschatological boundary sort people just as the section’s حِجْر restrains and distinguishes.
The alternation of night and day is a sign for أُو۟لِى ٱلْأَلْبَٰبِ, closely matching an oath from night and dawn addressed to the possessor of حِجْر.
Night, day, sun, moon, and stars are subjected as signs for people who reason; the cosmic scene explicitly calls for the faculty the section names حِجْر.
God’s turning of night and day contains a lesson for people of sight, joining the moving cover to the perceiver whom the oath expects to discern it.
The alternation of night and day is called a sign for people who reason, directly pairing the section’s temporal scene with its “possessor of restraint.”
The people of the Fire say that listening or reasoning would have restrained them from their end; this is the failed moral function the section’s dictionary gives to حِجْر.
When divine manifestation makes the mountain دَكًّا, the same root as 89:21 joins crushing ground to a theophanic scene, closely anticipating the crushed earth before the Lord’s coming in 89:21–22.
The earth and mountains are lifted and crushed with one دَكَّة, the clearest repeated Last-Day use of the section’s d-k-k image.
The protective barrier becomes دَكَّآء when God’s promise comes true; this ayah brings the section’s wall and its crushing verb into one scene of a boundary levelled at the appointed time.
No soul knows what delight has been hidden for them; this explicitly states the section’s account of Paradise as a reward still covered from present sight.
“Yā ʿibādī” addresses God’s servants with freedom from fear and grief, the closest external summons to the peaceful soul invited among “My servants” at the surah’s end.
“Enter the Garden” addresses those servants directly, reproducing the section’s final movement from divine call to entry into the garden-cover.
ٱدْخُلُوهَا بِسَلَٰمٍ commands entry into the near Garden in peace, closely matching the tranquil soul’s final invitation to enter.
The one who fears standing before the Lord and restrains the نفس from desire enacts the inner wall that the section says prevents unfitting action.
For the self restrained in 79:40, Paradise is the refuge; the pair joins the section’s inward حِجْر to the final garden shelter.
The soul is inspired with its فُجُور and its taqwā; this makes the section’s moral “tearing” one side of an explicit inward boundary.
The success of the one who purifies the soul states what happens when the inward boundary named in 91:8 is kept rather than torn.
The loss of the one who buries or corrupts the soul gives the dark reversal of purification and resonates with the section’s meeting of moral rupture and burial-cover.
The ayah refuses to equate corrupters with believers or the God-conscious with ٱلْفُجَّارِ; it joins 89:11–12’s فساد to the section’s فجر/فجور opposition.
God causes the human being to die and be buried; this is the explicit Qur’anic scene corresponding to the section’s secondary “grave-cover” sense.
The earth splits open from the dead as they hasten out, reversing burial-cover through an opening strikingly like dawn’s rent in darkness.
The earth casts out what is within it and becomes empty, turning the section’s covered grave-earth inside out at the Last Day.
The earth brings out its burdens, another direct uncovering of what burial had hidden beneath the ground.
When the graves are overturned and scattered, the grave-cover named in the section ceases to conceal its occupants.
God’s servants drink from a spring they make gush forth (يُفَجِّرُونَهَا تَفْجِيرًا); the f-j-r burst and “servants” meet on the garden side of the section’s closing image.
The promised Garden has lasting fruit and lasting shade; its enduring shade makes concrete the section’s derivation of janna from trees covering the ground.
In the garden reward, its shade is drawn close over them; the garden’s cover is experienced as shelter rather than the darkness or soil-cover left behind.
Every نفس tastes death, and success is being removed from the Fire and admitted to the Garden; one ayah traces the section’s passage from death-cover to garden entry.
God takes people during the night and raises them again by day; the nightly cover becomes a small death whose removal restores wakeful life.
God takes the الأنفس at death and during sleep, retains one and releases another; this directly binds the closing نفس to concealment, return, and the death threshold.
God makes night enter day and day enter night, then brings living from dead; the section’s two moving edges and its grave-to-life transition appear together.
God makes night enter day and day enter night; the reciprocal دخول renders their boundary as continual passage rather than a fixed line.
The mutual entry of night and day shows each cover sliding into the other, a direct analogue for night going and leaving what it covered exposed.
The entry of night into day and day into night stages the section’s opening and closing movements as two directions of one governed transition.
God makes night enter day and day enter night; its language of entry also echoes the final command to enter the garden after the night-image has passed.
Day cannot overtake night and each travels in an orbit; this supplies the firm boundary within which the section’s cover and dawn-opening succeed one another.
The question about a perpetual night asks who could bring light, exposing what dawn’s opening gives by imagining the cover never lifted.
The question about perpetual day asks who could bring a night for rest, preventing the section’s dawn from making darkness merely negative.
Night for rest and day for seeking bounty are paired mercies; their distinct gifts explain why the boundary between cover and disclosure must keep moving.
Those in the graves rush from them toward their Lord, directly continuing the section’s contrast between the earth-cover and the soul’s call toward God.
“Enter them in peace, secure” is a direct garden-entry command whose safety clarifies the sheltering quality of the section’s final cover.
The angels take the good in death saying “Peace” and “Enter the Garden,” explicitly joining the soul’s death-transition, peace, and entry.
“Enter the Garden; no fear upon you, nor shall you grieve” closely parallels the reassured addressee summoned into the final garden.
The righteous are told at the Garden’s gates to enter and remain; the threshold makes the section’s final دخول a visible crossing into enclosure.
The slain believer is told “Enter the Garden,” a compact instance of the section’s movement from death to the covered reward.
God strips day from night and people are left in darkness; this reverses the section’s dawn-image, where darkness is the layer removed and light appears beneath it.
Eyes that were under a covering from remembrance could not see; unlike Abraham’s night-cover, this inward cover prevents the very discernment darkness enabled for him.
Barriers before and behind plus a covering over sight leave people unable to see; it is an imposed wall that blinds, opposite the inward حِجْر that enables right judgment.
At death the wrongdoer asks to be sent back; this desperate, refused return contrasts with the peaceful soul’s welcomed return to its Lord, completed by the barrier in 23:100.
A barzakh stands behind the dead until resurrection, making the grave an uncrossable interim boundary rather than the open garden-entry offered to the tranquil soul.
The نفس that commands evil is the moral opposite of the tranquil soul; it shows why an inward restraint is needed before the final invitation.
The self-reproaching نفس stands between moral rupture and tranquillity, providing a distinct self-state against which the section’s final addressee can be heard.
The deniers cannot enter the Garden until a camel passes through a needle’s eye; garden entry here is barred, illuminating the unimpeded command at the surah’s end.
The righteous are in bliss, the immediate bright counterpart to the فُجَّار in 82:14 and therefore to the section’s warning that moral tearing does not release light.
حِجْر here is a humanly invented ban on crops and cattle; this secondary use is a caution that an external prohibition can masquerade as the sound inward restraint praised in the section.
God shows Abraham the dominion of heavens and earth so that he may have certainty; it states the purpose of the night-sky discernment enacted in 6:76–79.
The setting moon repeats the test first made with the star, showing that the night-cover permits a sequence of comparisons rather than one isolated sight.
The rising and then setting sun carries Abraham’s test across the dawn boundary into daylight, and its setting prevents daylight’s greater brightness from being confused with permanence.
Abraham turns toward the Creator of heavens and earth after the setting lights; this supplies the non-setting referent toward which the covered-night observations lead.
This ayah identifies the addressed servants as those who believed and submitted, specifying who receives the no-fear summons of 43:68 and entry command of 43:70.
The near Garden is promised to every returning, guarding person; “returning” and “guarding” join the final return to God with the section’s inward restraint.
Coming with a penitent heart while fearing the Merciful unseen explains the inner disposition immediately before “Enter it in peace” in 50:34.
The oath by the نفس and the One who proportioned it begins the passage that places فجور and taqwā within the soul, linking the section’s final addressee to its moral rupture.
Twilight is sworn by as the visible threshold before the oath turns to night and what it gathers, making the edge between light and cover perceptible.
The night “and what it gathers” portrays darkness as an enclosing container, a close variant of the section’s cover spread over things.
The full moon is the luminous object gathered within the night of 84:17, paralleling the visible star inside Abraham’s covering darkness.
The appointment of forty nights is another explicit counting of successive darknesses, though it lacks 7:142’s separate ten-night completion.
Prayer is marked from the sun’s decline through night’s darkness to قُرْءَانَ ٱلْفَجْرِ; dawn again serves as a witnessed liturgical boundary.
“Before the dawn prayer” and “after the night prayer” define two privacy thresholds, showing how dawn and night boundaries order embodied daily life.
Those seeking forgiveness in the pre-dawn hours inhabit the last thin portion of the night just before the section’s opening rent.
Seeking forgiveness at the pre-dawn hours gives the retreating end of night a specific devotional action before light appears.
The two edges of day and near portions of night divide worship across the same moving light-dark boundaries the section stages.
Glorification at night and at the retreat of the stars marks the observable moment when the night-cover and its lights withdraw together.
Night is made for rest and day for sight; the functional contrast clarifies darkness as shelter without treating it as mere blindness.
Night provides repose while day gives sight, repeating the complementary uses of cover and disclosure for people who can perceive the sign.
God makes night for rest and day sight-giving; the recurrent pair supports the section’s distinction between a useful cover and its illuminating removal.
Sleep is made for repose immediately before night is called a garment, adding the death-like stillness that the section later sets beside burial.
Day is made for livelihood immediately after night’s garment, giving the uncovered interval its active human purpose.
The alternation of night and day appears among signs for people who reason; the broader catalogue still concretely echoes the oath’s appeal to a discerning mind.
The alternation of night and day and what God created within them are signs for the mindful, another explicit audience for the same cosmic transition.
People pass the ruins of the destroyed community in the morning; daylight exposes the remnant of transgression, much as the section’s dawn precedes its ruined peoples.
They also pass the ruins at night and are asked whether they will reason, joining night, destroyed transgressors, and the section’s appeal to inward understanding.
Lot’s family is saved at the last pre-dawn hour, making the receding edge of night the boundary between refuge and judgment.
A lasting punishment overtakes the people in the morning, the judgment-side of the dawn boundary whose saving side appears in 54:34.
The decree that the people will be cut off by morning makes dawn the fixed terminus of the family’s night journey in 15:65.
The blast seizes the people at sunrise, disclosing the destructive outcome that lay beyond the commanded night departure.
The owners swear to harvest their garden in the morning; a garden and an anticipated dawn are deliberately placed in one test-scene.
A visitation circles the garden while its owners sleep, so the night-cover conceals a decisive change from human sight.
By morning the garden has become like a dark, stripped field; dawn reveals loss where the section’s final Garden promises shelter.
The owners call one another at morning, moving from the hidden event of 68:19 to human recognition after light returns.
Water bursts from struck rock as twelve springs; the section’s f-j-r root here names a physical rupture through a hard cover rather than dawn through darkness.
Rocks from which rivers burst show the same f-j-r mechanism in matter: what was enclosed breaks outward through stone.
The demand that a spring be made to gush from the earth uses the section’s f-j-r root for an opening through ground rather than night.
God makes a river gush between two gardens; the physical f-j-r branch and the garden-cover meet in a single cultivated scene.
The earth is burst into springs until waters meet for a decreed event, enlarging the root-image from a slit of light to openings across the ground.
The seas are burst open at the cosmic end; the f-j-r root carries rupture from dawn’s life-giving light to an overwhelming eschatological release.
The heavens and earth were joined and then split apart, a cosmic nonlexical parallel to a concealed expanse opened by a decisive cleft.
The sea splits after Moses strikes it, supplying the opened path that answers the commanded night journey in 26:52.
The earth is split open so growth can emerge; like dawn, an enclosing surface parts and what was hidden beneath becomes manifest.
The human wants to continue in فُجُور ahead of him; this is the section’s moral f-j-r branch as an ongoing breach of limits rather than a release of light.
Clothing covers nakedness while “the garment of taqwā” is better; it gives Qur’anic form to the section’s dictionary metaphor of a religious cover that فجور tears.
The فُجَّار are in blazing fire, showing that the moral rupture sharing dawn’s root opens onto punishment rather than illumination.
The record of the فُجَّار is in Sijjīn; the moral tearing named in the section is here fixed into a constricting record and destination.
The two seas are released to meet, establishing the moving bodies whose non-transgression is explained by the barrier in 55:20.
Between the meeting seas is a barrier they do not transgress; this is a concrete outward model of restraint holding movement within its proper limit.
The God-conscious are amid gardens and springs immediately before the command to enter safely, presenting the garden as an encompassing place of shelter.
The righteous enter Gardens of Eden with flowing rivers and fulfilled desires; it supplies the concealed reward into which 16:32’s death-time greeting admits them.
The righteous enter Gardens of Eden together with righteous kin, expanding the final invitation “among My servants” into a gathered community.
Angels enter upon them through every gate with a greeting of peace, making the garden boundary permeable to welcome rather than exclusion.
Angels descend on the steadfast at death with “do not fear or grieve” and glad tidings of the promised Garden, closely echoing the reassurance around the final soul-call.
Gardens of refuge (جَنَّاتُ ٱلْمَأْوَىٰ) are the believers’ lodging, explicitly presenting Paradise as the sheltering cover developed in the section.
The two gardens are described as possessing spreading branches, supporting the section’s lexical picture of a garden whose trees cover what lies beneath.
Extended shade in the reward scene isolates the sheltering function that the section hears within the word janna.
The people of the Garden and their spouses recline in shade, making the final cover a place of rest and companionship.
The God-conscious are amid shades and springs; protective cover and released water meet as favorable counterparts to the section’s garden and bursting images.
God will raise those in the graves, stating the promised reversal of the earth-cover whose physical opening other Last-Day ayat depict.
People emerge from the graves with lowered eyes like scattered locusts, giving movement and visibility to what had been hidden under burial.
They rush from the graves as though toward a marker, another explicit transition from enclosed earth to exposed assembly.
What is in the graves is scattered out, a forceful uncovering of the section’s grave sense of the covering root.
Humans are created from earth, returned into it, and brought out again; the whole sequence distinguishes temporary soil-cover from final emergence.
Human growth from the earth like vegetation links the opened ground to life and anticipates return beneath that same surface.
God returns people into the earth and brings them out again, making burial-cover a passage rather than their lasting enclosure.
God removes Job’s affliction; it is a concrete Qur’anic counterpart to the section’s secondary dictionary example of worry being lifted away as a cover clears.
God answers the distressed and removes evil, preserving the section’s secondary “anxiety lifted” sense as an experienced release rather than a visual dawn.
Those who listen and follow the best word are the people of understanding; the ayah describes how the inward faculty called حِجْر actually restrains choice.
The stars guide through the darknesses of land and sea; like Abraham's star, a light within darkness makes orientation possible instead of merely being obscured by the cover.
God covers day with night, then calls these signs for people who reflect; this repeats both the moving cover and the discerning audience of the section's oath.
Night, day, sun, and moon are signs, but people must worship their Creator rather than the luminaries; this states the theological discrimination enacted by Abraham under night-cover.
The barrier placed between two seas repeats the section's outward model for حِجْر: a boundary that prevents two moving domains from overrunning one another.
A veil separates the people of the Garden and Fire while those on the heights recognize both groups, joining eschatological boundary, discernment, and the hoped-for Garden.
The lote tree stands at the furthest boundary, bringing an actual tree and a terminal limit together immediately beside the Garden of Refuge.
The Garden of Refuge lies beside the boundary-tree, making Paradise explicitly an enclosing shelter at a limit.
The lote tree is covered by what covers it, an unusually direct meeting of tree, covering action, and the adjacent Garden whose name the section derives from cover.
Believers are admitted to gardens and into deep, abundant shade; the ayah explicitly combines garden-entry with the sheltering cover developed in the section.
God rewards patience with a Garden and silk, identifying the garden scene whose close shade is described in 76:14 as recompense.
No weariness touches the Garden's people and they will never be made to leave it; permanent non-exit sharpens the section's dictionary contrast between دخول and خروج.
Every soul tastes death and then returns to God, reproducing the closing soul's death-threshold and return before 29:58 supplies its Garden lodging.
Believers are lodged in lofty chambers of the Garden after the soul's death and return in 29:57, completing the same movement from mortality into shelter.
At one divine call people come out of the earth; this closely reverses grave-cover and parallels the soul being summoned toward its Lord.
The sky is split open at the Last Day, extending the section's opening rent from the edge of night to the whole celestial cover before seas and graves also open.
After sky, sea, and graves open, every soul knows what it sent ahead and left behind; the cosmic rupture culminates in uncovered self-knowledge.
The sky splits open at the start of the passage whose earth later spreads and casts out its contents, pairing an opened upper cover with the uncovered grave-earth.
The earth is convulsed violently, beginning a three-ayah dissolution of ground and mountains that closely parallels the dakk scene.
The mountains are pulverized completely, supplying the crushing action that follows the earth's convulsion in 56:4.
The pulverized mountains become scattered dust, showing the exposed residue after the stable earthly cover has been broken down.
The shaking earth and mountains reduced to a loose heap of sand form a close physical parallel to the earth's repeated pounding in 89:21.
God will blast the mountains away, initiating an explicit removal of the earth's raised features before the level plain of 20:106–107.
The removed mountains leave a level, bare plain, a direct scene-parallel to the ground made flat by dakk.
No crookedness or elevation remains visible in the plain, stating the completed levelling contributed by the preceding mountain-removal.
Satan expels Adam's parents from the Garden while stripping their clothing to expose them; garden-exit and lost cover become one moral reversal of the section's final entry into shelter.
Night, day, sun, and moon each travel in an orbit, giving cosmic motion to the same succession that the section pictures as a travelling night.
The moon's measured phases disclose the number of years and calculation; it connects visible nocturnal light with the section's counting of successive nights.

After a people's strongholds fail and their dwellings are ruined, the audience is told to take warning, O people of sight; this matches Surah 89's destroyed peoples addressed to one capable of discernment.
The histories of earlier peoples contain a lesson for people of understanding, directly explaining how Surah 89's destruction narratives answer its question to the possessor of حِجْر.
The moon itself is split as the Hour approaches; instead of darkness cracking to disclose a light, a visible night-light becomes the object of rupture.
Layered darkness in the deep sea leaves a person barely able to see even a raised hand; this marks the limit where darkness ceases to aid discrimination and overwhelms sight.
Faces covered with pieces of dark night turn the section's sheltering natural cover into an image of humiliation and punishment.
Satan causes the pair to slip and brings them out of the Garden; this forced خروج is the narrative reverse of the closing invitation to enter God's Garden.
The arrogant are commanded to enter Hell's gates immediately before the righteous enter the Garden in 39:73; the same threshold-action leads to opposite enclosures.
God guides people through the darknesses of land and sea, another specific instance in which darkness contains the means of finding a way rather than abolishing perception.
The reward contains thornless lote trees, supplying one part of the actual tree-canopy behind the extended shade named in 56:30.
Layered acacia or banana trees add the second concrete canopy immediately before the passage names extended shade.
Those reclining in the Garden see neither burning sun nor bitter cold, specifying what the close shade of 76:14 shelters them from.
The promised Gardens of Eden belong to the unseen, directly supporting the section's claim that the garden reward is presently hidden yet certain to arrive.
Within the promised reward, people receive whatever their souls desire; the closing نفس and its still-hidden delight meet in the continuation of 41:30's death-time reassurance.
The promised delights are a welcoming provision from the Forgiving, Merciful, characterizing the hidden Garden as hospitality after the angels' reassurance.
After the command to enter the Garden, it contains what souls desire and eyes delight in, unfolding the concealed joy promised to the final soul.
Every soul tastes death, is tested, and returns to God; it preserves the section's sequence from نفس through death-cover to return, though it does not itself name the Garden.
Every soul arrives with a driver and witness immediately before its covering is removed in 50:22, identifying whose final perception is uncovered.
Every soul knows what it has brought before the oaths by the retreating night and breathing morning, so the cosmic uncovering frames an inward disclosure.
Every soul is held in pledge for what it earned shortly after the oaths by departing night and brightening morning, linking the dawn scene to moral accountability.
The sky splits and becomes frail on the day when earth and mountains have been crushed, continuing the dakk scene from ground to celestial cover.
The one hiding by night is set against the one moving openly by day, giving the natural cover a concrete human use and daylight its disclosure.
God measures the varying portions of night and day while worshippers stand through them, linking successive nights to exact temporal measure.
Glorification before sunrise and sunset, during portions of night, and at the day's ends marks the same perceptible thresholds the section's oaths stage.
The command to glorify before sunrise and before sunset turns the two light-boundaries into moments of addressed attention.
Glorification during the night continues the boundary-command of 50:39 through the covering interval itself.
The command to glorify God at evening and morning explicitly places worship at the passage into and out of night.
Praise at late day and noon completes 30:17's morning-evening frame, spreading remembrance across the cycle's visible stages.
No one but God can remove affliction; this is a direct Qur'anic counterpart to the source section's secondary dictionary example of anxiety lifting away.
In distress people call on God and He removes what prompted the call if He wills, enacting the section's secondary sense of a burden being uncovered.
If harm touches a person none but God can remove it, a repeated formulation of the section's nonvisual “worry lifted” branch.
When God removes harm, the affliction passes like a lifted cover, though the ayah warns that some then associate partners with Him.
Invoked beings cannot remove or transfer harm, setting a boundary around who can perform the release illustrated by the section's lifted-anxiety example.
False objects of worship cannot remove harm God intends, again distinguishing the true agent who can lift what weighs upon a person.
When punishment descends into a people's courtyard, it is called an evil morning for those warned; dawn here discloses judgment rather than relief.
The people are told to travel safely through the linked settlements by nights and days, a nonlexical parallel to night as a traversed interval.
Dense, luxuriant gardens emerge in the sequence begun by the earth's splitting in 80:26, joining a rent in the ground to the tree-cover it produces.
Rain brings varied fruits from dead land and becomes an analogy for bringing out the dead, joining growing cover above the earth with release from beneath it.
